title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time and the day, make arrangements, and face the one point that trips up almost every beginner: *pol siedmej* means "half to seven", and that's 6:30.
bekal: tell the time in two ways: the official style and the conversational style
use *o* + an ordinal form to say "at what time"
name the days and say when something happens

notes: **Pol ôsmej = 7:30, not 8:30.** This is the point that makes people miss appointments in Slovakia most often. Slovak counts **toward** the next hour: *pol ôsmej* literally means "half of the eighth" — halfway on the way to eight o'clock. German and Hungarian do the same; English doesn't.

**English speakers, beware.** In British English "half eight" means 8:30 — the opposite direction. Slovak *pol ôsmej* is 7:30. If you think in "half past", translate the Slovak in your head as "half **to**" eight.

**Štvrť na osem = 7:15.** Literally "a quarter toward eight" — counting forward again. And *trištvrte na osem* = 7:45, "three quarters toward eight". All three forms (*štvrť na*, *pol*, *trištvrte na*) count toward the next hour, no exceptions.
**O koľkej?** = "at what time?" The form *koľkej* is feminine locative, because the dropped word *hodina* (hour) is feminine. Every way of saying the time uses the feminine for the same reason.

**V piatok takes the accusative, not the locative.** Odd, since *v* usually wants the locative — but for days, Slovak uses the accusative: *v pondelok, v stredu, v sobotu*. Ten seconds to learn, and it lasts a lifetime.

grammars.title: Telling the time — two styles
body: Slovak has an official style (train timetables, the news, doctor's appointments) and a conversational style. The first is easy; the second is the one that needs practice.
after: **The official style uses the 24-hour clock and plain numbers** — just like a digital display. When in doubt, use this: it's always correct and never misunderstood.

**The conversational style uses the 12-hour clock** and relies on ordinal forms ("the seventh", "the eighth"). This is what you'll hear from friends, and what you need to recognize even before you dare to use it.
**There are two questions**: *Koľko je hodín?* (what time is it now) and *O koľkej?* (at what time does something happen). Don't mix them up — the first asks the time, the second asks for a schedule.

grammars.title: O + ordinal: at what time
body: To say "at … o'clock", Slovak uses *o* followed by a feminine ordinal in the locative. It sounds complicated; the table covers everything.
after: **They all end in *-ej*** because they're all feminine locative. Once you see that pattern, you only need to learn the stems: *jedn-, druh-, tret-, štvrt-, piat-, šiest-, siedm-, ôsm-, deviat-, desiat-*.

**The last column is where the trap is.** *Pol* always pairs with the **next** hour. To say half past six (6:30), you have to say **seven**: *pol siedmej*. Read that column aloud a few times; it won't feel natural until you do.
**Morning or evening?** Add *ráno*, *popoludní*, *večer*, or *v noci*: *o siedmej ráno* (7 a.m.), *o siedmej večer* (7 p.m.). In everyday speech people often drop it when the context makes it clear.

blocks.text: The last column isn't just a story: it makes all seven almost unnecessary to memorize. The Slovak week **starts on Monday**, so *utorok* is the second day, *streda* is in the middle, *štvrtok* the fourth, *piatok* the fifth. And *nedeľa* — from *ne-delať*, "not working" — explains why *pondelok* means "after nedeľa".

The Slovak month names are borrowed from Latin, so you already know them all. That's unlike Czech and Polish, which use native Slavic month names (*leden, únor* in Czech) that have to be learned one by one. A small gift from history.

*Zima* means winter **and** cold: *Je mi zima* = "I'm cold". Likewise *leto* — summer and, in old-fashioned counting, a year. Notice that two seasons take *na* and two take *v*; this is pure habit and has to be learned in pairs.

blocks.title: Punctuality in Slovakia
items: Social arrangements are kept to within five minutes. Arriving fifteen minutes late without warning is considered rude, and arriving at someone's home **early** is even worse — the host may not be ready.
If you're running late, send a message: *Meškám desať minút, prepáč.* That one sentence settles the whole thing.
For official appointments — the doctor, an office, an interview — arrive five minutes early. Counters in Slovakia really do close at the time written on the door.
